2611.23643.title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars

figures.caption: Figure 1: Modular structure of MAIC-2 v2.3. All initializations are done in the main program maic2. This includes reading the physical parameters and the set-up from the run-specs header file maic2_specs_<run_name>.h, where <run_name> is a placeholder for the name of the simulation to be carried out. In the main loop (numerical forward-in-time integration), maic2 carries out three steps: (1) Use the module boundary_maic2_m to update the orbital parameters, compute the surface temperature (LIT scheme, module instemp_m) and the surface mass balance for H2O ice (evaporation, atmospheric water transport and condensation, module evap_cond_m); (2) use the module calc_top_maic2_m to update the topography (thickness) of the H2O ice deposits; (3) use the module output_m for data output in ASCII format. Auxiliary modules are maic2_types_m for declarations of kind types, maic2_variables_m for declarations of global variables, and maic2_maths_m for required mathematical tools.
Figure 2: Obliquity from $20\>\mathrm{Ma}$ ago until $10\>\mathrm{Ma}$ into the future (Laskar et al. 2004).
Figure 3: Distribution of the atmospheric water content $\omega$ relative to the value at the south pole, $\omega_{\mathrm{SP}}$, with a prescribed north-south gradient.

Figure 4: Simulations #6 (top panels) and #39 (bottom panels): Volume of the north-polar and south-polar layered deposits ($V_{\mathrm{NPLD}}$, $V_{\mathrm{SPLD}}$; polewards of $75^{\circ}\mathrm{N/S}$), and ice thickness at the respective poles ($H_{\mathrm{NP}}$, $H_{\mathrm{SP}}$).

The ice thicknesses are exaggerated by a factor 750 relative to the size of the planet. (For a supplementary animation of the time-dependent glaciation, see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3700636.)

Figure 6: Simulation #40: Volume of the north-polar and south-polar layered deposits ($V_{\mathrm{NPLD}}$, $V_{\mathrm{SPLD}}$; polewards of $75^{\circ}\mathrm{N/S}$), and ice thickness at the respective poles ($H_{\mathrm{NP}}$, $H_{\mathrm{SP}}$).

2611.23643.abstract: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

2611.23818.title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the NEXOTRANS framework [12], showing the forward-modeling component (green box), existing retrieval methods (purple box), and the NEXONN framework introduced in this work (gray box). The forward model generates transmission spectra by solving the radiative-transfer equation for specified atmospheric properties, including chemical composition, pressure–temperature structure, and cloud prescriptions. The existing retrieval module includes Bayesian sampling methods such as PyMultiNest and UltraNest, together with the machine-learning-based Stacking Regressor, which combines Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and K-Nearest Neighbors. NEXONN extends this framework using TcNF to perform probabilistic posterior estimation of atmospheric parameters.

Figure 2: Schematic representation of the NEXONN training framework. Synthetic spectra, $\mathbf{x}$, are generated using NEXOTRANS [12], with PandExo-based noise realizations incorporated during training to represent wavelength-dependent observational uncertainties. The resulting spectra are processed by the transformer, which provides the conditioning representation for the NF. The flow learns the invertible transformation between the atmospheric parameter space and the latent distribution. Training is performed by minimizing the NF negative log-likelihood given in Equation 4.

Figure 3: Comparison of the transmission spectra corresponding to the PyMultiNest (purple) and NEXONN (orange) retrievals for the simulated JWST MIRI/LRS experiment. The simulated observations were generated using the NEXOTRANS forward model with PandExo-based noise. Both retrievals are performed on the same simulated dataset with known input atmospheric parameters.

Figure 4: Comparison of the posterior distributions retrieved with PyMultiNest (green) and NEXONN (purple) for the simulated spectrum generated using the NEXOTRANS forward model with PandExo-based noise. The black markers indicate the true values of the atmospheric parameters used to generate the simulated spectrum.

Figure 5: Comparison of the retrieved JWST MIRI/LRS transmission spectra of WASP-39 b using PyMultiNest (orange) and NEXONN (purple). The observations are based on the Powell et al. [46] reduction performed with the Eureka! pipeline. The retrieval model assumes Free Chemistry, an isothermal pressure–temperature (P–T) profile, haze, and patchy-gray clouds. The 28 observed spectral points are shown in black. The lower panel shows the residuals relative to the observed transit depths.

Figure 6: The figure shows the corner plots comparing the posterior distributions retrieved using PyMultiNest (blue), NEXONN with PandExo noise (purple) for JWST MIRI (5 - 12$\mu$m) observed spectrum of WASP-39 b, reduced using Eureka! pipeline [46].

Figure 7: Comparison of the retrieved transmission spectra of WASP-39 b over the full JWST wavelength range of $0.6$–$12\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ using PyMultiNest (yellow) and NEXONN (purple). The NEXONN model was trained using PandExo-based noise realizations. The retrieval adopts the Hybrid Equilibrium Chemistry model together with a uniform cloud and aerosol prescription.
Figure 8: Comparison of the posterior distributions obtained with PyMultiNest (blue) and NEXONN (purple) for the full JWST transmission spectrum of WASP-39 b spanning $0.6$–$12\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.

Figure 9: Retrieved pressure–temperature (P–T) profiles for the full JWST transmission spectrum of WASP-39 b using the Hybrid Equilibrium Chemistry model. The PyMultiNest and NEXONN results are shown in yellow and purple, respectively.
Figure 10: Mass–metallicity relation showing the atmospheric metallicity inferred for WASP-39 b using PyMultiNest and NEXONN.

2611.23818.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Complex matrix diagrams for the three different four-input combiner modes at a wavelength of $3.75$ $\mu$m. Top: Single-Bracewell mode. Mid: Symmetric dual-Bracewell mode. Bottom: Asymmetric dual-Bracewell mode. Each arrow represents the transmission of light from an input to the shown output, with its direction indicating the relative phase orientation of the beams at the outputs of the beam combiner, and its length indicating the relative intensity. The relative phase of $\pi/2$ between the photometric outputs 0 and 1, as well as between outputs 6 and 7, results from phase offsets applied to the input beams before the beam combiner, which compensate the $\pi/2$ phase shift imposed by the directional couplers on the cross-coupled light, and does not affect the measured intensities. The vector sum of all arrows at a given output determines the resulting interference of the transmitted light. 2611.24397.abstract: Near-infrared interferometric surveys have revealed extended emission around the photosphere of $\approx 40$ main-sequence stars, attributed to the presence of hot exozodiacal dust (HEZD). A promising technique for investigating this phenomenon is nulling interferometry. The Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) nulling interferometer NOTT (Nulling Observations of exoplaneTs and dusT) is designed to characterise exoplanets and HEZD in the $L'$ band ($3.5-4.0\,\mu$m). We aim to assess NOTT's potential for the detection and characterisation of HEZD with various instrumental and model parameter configurations. We model the HEZD as an optically thin dust ring, using the nearby Sun-like star $\tau$ Ceti with HEZD as a reference model. Applying the end-to-end nulling tool SCIFYsim to model the instrumental response of NOTT to simulated HEZD brightness distributions, we evaluate how variations in HEZD and instrumental parameters affect NOTT's key observables: the photon flux rate and the null depth. We demonstrate that NOTT is capable of disentangling stellar and dust contributions to the signal and detecting HEZD. The null depth and photon flux rate are sensitive to the HEZD geometry, with inclination, position angle, and ring location having the strongest impact on the signal. Although the detailed temporal signatures are target-specific, the results can be generalised to other systems. NOTT has the potential to deliver unprecedented sensitivity for HEZD observations, granting access to detailed information through spectral dispersion, beam-combination schemes, and exploitation of sky rotation. This enables more sensitive HEZD detections than is possible with current instruments, and improved spatial constraints on the dust, as well as variability studies.

2611.24416.abstract: Almost negligible among the solar system planets, mutual tides raised by a secondary on another secondary orbiting the same primary may gain increased importance in tightly packed systems, e.g., between the components of close-in exoplanetary systems or between the moons of gas giants. In this work, we derive an analytical formula for the planet-planet tidal potential and for the effect of mutual tides on the rotational and orbital evolution of moons or planets in a coplanar configuration. The procedure follows closely the steps of W. M. Kaula (1961), and the resulting potential and derived quantities are presented in the form of an expansion into modes of different frequencies (in the temporal domain) and spherical harmonic components (in the spatial domain). The analytical formulae are implemented into a code and compared with an independent numerical solution.

2611.24615.title: Thermodynamics of gas giants accreting via shocks: the role of molecular hydrogen dissociation

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic diagram of the hydrodynamic processes in our model. Gas infalls at free-fall velocity from the outer boundary of the computational domain (defined in Sect. 2.1.3) and forms an accretion shock at the top of the planetary atmosphere, after which the shocked gas cools and settles onto deeper layers. Here, $L_{\mathrm{int}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{acc}}$ denote the internal luminosity from the planetary interior and the accretion luminosity, respectively.

Figure 2: Representative steady-state accretion shock solution from Guangqi for a gas giant with $M_{\mathrm{p}}=1\,\mathrm{M_{J}}$, $R_{\mathrm{in}}=2\,\mathrm{R_{J}}$, $\dot{M}=0.005\,\mathrm{M_{\oplus}\,yr^{-1}}$, and $L_{\mathrm{int}}/L_{\mathrm{acc}}=0.1$. Panels show radial profiles of (a) gas velocity, (b) density, (c) pressure, (d) Planck mean opacity (blue) and Rosseland mean opacity (red), (e) radiation temperature (blue) and gas temperature (red), (f) reduced radiation flux, (g) luminosity, (h) specific entropy, and (i) $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ mass fraction. Open circles mark the post-shock state.

Figure 3: Post-shock specific entropy $S_{\mathrm{ps}}$ as a function of initial planetary radius $R_{\mathrm{in}}$ across varying accretion rates $\dot{M}$ (colors). Columns from left to right correspond to $M_{\mathrm{p}}=\{0.3,1,3\}\,\mathrm{M_{J}}$, and rows correspond to $L_{\mathrm{int}}/L_{\mathrm{acc}}=\{0.1,0.3\}$. Filled squares denote simulations in which the post-shock atomic hydrogen mass fraction exceeds $\chi_{\mathrm{H,ps}}>2\%$. The upper x-axis indicates the critical accretion rate $\dot{M}_{\mathrm{crit}}$ (Eq. 17) corresponding to each combination of $M_{\mathrm{p}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{in}}$.

Figure 4: Effect of dust opacity on post-shock specific entropy for a $M_{\mathrm{p}}=0.3\,\mathrm{M_{J}}$ gas giant at $\dot{M}=0.001\,\mathrm{M_{\oplus}\,yr^{-1}}$ (left) and $\dot{M}=0.01\,\mathrm{M_{\oplus}\,yr^{-1}}$ (right). Solid lines adopt the fiducial dust opacity of Semenov et al. (2003), whereas dashed lines adopt half that opacity with all other parameters fixed. The two curves overlap completely in the right panel.

Figure 5: Architecture of the physics-informed neural network (PINN). Alongside the primary inputs, the physics-guided feature $M_{\mathrm{p}}/R_{\mathrm{in}}$ (orange) is supplied to the input layer. Within the dense hidden layers, the post-shock density $\rho_{\mathrm{ps}}$ (green) is incorporated as a supervised latent variable. A customized physics-informed loss function $\mathcal{L}$ (red) replaces the standard MSE objective. Depending on the EoS formulation in $\mathcal{L}$, the output layer returns either $[S_{\mathrm{ps}},T_{\mathrm{ps}},\chi_{\mathrm{H,ps}}]$ or $[S_{\mathrm{ps}},T_{\mathrm{ps}},P_{\mathrm{ps}}]$.

2611.24615.abstract: Within the core-accretion framework, gas giants acquire most of their mass through accretion shocks during runaway gas accretion. The shock thermodynamics---governed by radiative cooling, accretion history, and equation of state (EoS)---sets the post-shock gas entropy and initial thermal state, strongly influencing both observables and subsequent evolution. We aim to build a coupled evolutionary model predicting the initial thermodynamic conditions, intrinsic luminosities, and upper limits on magnetic field strengths of gas giants across diverse accretion histories. We couple radiation hydrodynamics and $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociation to long-term planetary interior evolution by training a physics-informed neural network (PINN) predictor on 1000 first-principles simulations resolving the shock physics. This PINN provides post-shock outer boundary conditions for MESA to evolve the planetary envelope beyond runaway accretion. The PINN predicts higher post-shock temperatures than the canonical cold-start model, with the discrepancy widening with planetary mass, while post-shock entropy jumps sharply when $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociates at $\sim 2000$ K. Gas giants evolved with PINN-derived boundary conditions achieve intrinsic luminosities 4--10 times higher than cold-start models. Under optimistic assumptions, the maximum magnetic field strength at $2 R_{\mathrm{J}}$ reaches a few gauss for a $0.3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$ planet, $\sim 100$ G for $1 M_{\mathrm{J}}$, and $\sim 500$ G for $3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$. Incorporating detailed radiation hydrodynamics and realistic thermodynamics into accretion shock models yields higher initial entropies, brighter intrinsic luminosities, and stronger magnetic fields, providing improved constraints on the masses and accretion rates of directly imaged exoplanets.

2611.24812.title: A Homogeneous Benchmark of Exoplanet Mass-Radius Relations

The intermediate mass range ($4.4\leq M<127\,M_{\oplus}$), where interior compositional degeneracy is strong, exhibits a broad spread in mass at fixed radius. Because the benchmark predicts mass from radius, predictive difficulty is governed by the horizontal dispersion in $\log_{10}M$ at a given $\log_{10}R$.

Figure 2: Mass-prediction RMSE stratified by method and planetary mass class. Because relative model rankings shift across the low-mass, intermediate-mass, and giant intervals, a single global RMSE does not fully characterize model performance.

Figure 3: Empirical versus nominal interval coverage on the test set, with horizontal offsets applied for visual clarity. Conformal ML intervals lie close to the diagonal across the full test set ($N=240$), whereas SPRIGHT is evaluated on the 96-planet subset within its validity domain ($0.5\leq R\leq 6.5\,R_{\oplus}$).
Figure 4: Permutation feature importance for RandomForest-multi on the held-out test set, measured as the increase in test RMSE (in dex) when each feature is randomly shuffled.

Figure 5: Residual log-mass distributions grouped by discovery method. The RV-discovered and other transit-discovered subsamples differ in median residual by $0.173\text{ dex}$ ($95\%$ bootstrap CI $[0.112,\,0.261]$; Section V.6).

2611.24812.abstract: The mass-radius ($M$-$R$) relation is fundamental to inferring the bulk composition and internal structure of exoplanets. However, published relations remain difficult to compare directly because studies adopt different planetary samples, fitting procedures, and evaluation metrics. We construct a homogeneous, quality-controlled benchmark of 963 exoplanets with dynamically measured masses and transit radii from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. We compare empirical power laws, probabilistic models, and machine-learning (ML) regressors using point accuracy, interval coverage, and probabilistic calibration. On the full test set, a multi-feature random forest has the lowest root-mean-square error, 0.329~dex in $\log_{10} M$ versus 0.368~dex for a fitted two-parameter power law ($p = 0.007$ unadjusted; $p = 0.059$ after Holm correction across 13 comparisons). Radius-only ML models perform comparably to the single power law. In three ranges of the measured radius, several methods improve on the power law below 1.6 $R_\oplus$, but none does between 1.6 and 4 $R_\oplus$. Including stellar and orbital covariates significantly improves predictions only for low-mass planets ($M < 4.4\,M_\oplus$), although this result is sensitive to missing covariate data and weakens when the training and test sets are separated by host star. Within their calibrated radius domains, the published empirical and probabilistic relations remain highly competitive. Finally, a first-order variance decomposition shows that formal measurement uncertainties account for only $\sim$3\% of the residual variance (0.067 of 0.401~dex), and the remaining $\sim$0.396~dex arises from compositional diversity, selection effects, and model approximation error.

The colour map indicates the density of posterior draws in a given hexagonal bin in semi-major axis and mass space. Marginalized histograms are shown to the top and right of the main plot, with a solid line indicating the median value and dashed lines at the 16th and 84th percentiles of the marginalized distributions.

Figure 4: Random subsample of 3000 G23H+RV posterior draws (for visual clarity) for the OC TOI-178 h in semi-major axis–mass space. In each panel, draws ruled out by a preceding constraint are shown faded, and those still allowed are outlined in black. (a) AO Spatial Resolution: Grey markers are posterior draws for which the imaging data give no constraint. Red points are draws tested against the AO contrast curves; faded red points are excluded by imaging or photometry. The solid line shows the Br$\gamma$ mass limit at 6 Gyr for reference. (b) Inner System Coupling: Secular coupling of the inner planets relative to each OC posterior draw following Lai and Pu [36]. Draws in the weak regime ($\epsilon_{j,f}^{max}>10$) would rapidly destabilise the inner system. (c) OC Libration Forcing: The colour map shows the ratio of the OC’s quadrupole forcing timescale, $t_{g,\mathrm{OC}}^{\mathrm{quad}}$, to the longest libration timescale of the inner resonant chain, $t_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\mathrm{lib}}$. Samples with ratio $<10$ are excluded. Gold squares mark draws where the quadrupole approximation is not valid. (d) N-body Simulations: Outcome of N-body integrations of the inner system plus OC over 60 $t_{g,\mathrm{OC}}^{\mathrm{quad}}$; purple diamonds represent simulations that became unstable over the integration time, and purple squares represent simulations that remain stable but do not librate at the end of the integration time.

The full G23H+RV posterior draws are shown as grey points. The surviving posterior draws are shaded according to fitted eccentricity. The marginalised semi-major axis and mass posteriors are shown for the G23H+RV (grey) and final (green) posteriors in the top and right axes, with vertical lines showing the median (solid) and 16th/84th percentiles (dashed). KDE contours at 68.3$\$\$\%$$$, 95.4%, and 99.7% are shown over the final posterior draws.

2611.24854.abstract: We report the discovery of a massive outer companion around TOI-178, a known planetary system with six inner small planets within 0.15 AU, five of which are in a 2:4:6:9:12 resonant chain. We analyse the astrometric anomalies in the combined Gaia DR2/DR3 - Hipparcos catalogue (G23H) and literature radial velocities, revealing strong evidence for a massive outer companion at several AU. We combine the resulting orbital fit posterior with archival high-contrast imaging to constrain the properties of the corresponding massive outer companion, TOI-178 h. We also study the dynamical stability of the inner resonant chain in the presence of this previously unknown outer companion via both heuristic and N-body simulations. We find that the inner system appears to be robust to the perturbing influence of TOI-178\,h, in line with the systems several Gyr age. Our analysis results in a final posterior solution for TOI-178\,h with a semi-major axis of $6.9^{+12.3}_{-3.3}$ AU, a mass of $21^{+47}_{-11} M_J$, and eccentricity of $0.76^{+0.18}_{-0.35}$, likely corresponding to an eccentric brown dwarf. TOI-178 is currently the only known system that has maintained a high-multiplicity resonant chain whilst in the dynamical presence of a massive outer companion, showcasing a unique outcome of planet formation.

2611.23393.abstract: Since 1969, Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) has provided critical data for investigating Earth-Moon dynamics, lunar internal structure, and tests of General Relativity (GR). However, the measurement precision of historical arrays (such as those from Apollo and Lunokhod missions) is inherently limited by laser pulse broadening induced by lunar librations. To overcome this limit, next-generation single Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs) of large optical diameter have been developed to eliminate pulse dispersion, enabling LLR measurements to advance from centimeter-level precision down to the millimeter scale. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of LLR observations from NGLR-1 (Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1), the first single 10cm-diameter CCR deployed on the lunar surface. Carried out using the Planetary Ephemeris Program (PEP), this study investigates individual range measurements, normal points (NPs), residuals, and observational dispersion collected by the ground stations at Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging station (APOL), Wettzell, and Grasse. The results: demonstrate the success of NGLR-1 in significantly enhancing time of flight measurement precision compared to legacy Apollo and Lunokhod retroreflector arrays; indicate similar good prospects also for ESA's MPAc laser retroreflector (MoonLIGHT with Pointing Actuators) to be launched in early 2027; pave the way for a new era of LLR observations and enhanced tests of GR, alternative gravity theories in general and improved lunar geophysics and geodesy.

2611.24020.abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the main oxidant in the troposphere and accounts for 88% of the methane sink, yet its abundance and trends remain poorly constrained. Satellites observe many of the chemical and meteorological drivers of OH, but assimilating both requires a model that represents chemistry and meteorology together. Existing chemistry-climate models are too expensive for joint data assimilation. Here, we present AuroraChem, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model that jointly simulates meteorology and the GEOS-Chem chemical fields needed to constrain OH. A one-year AuroraChem rollout takes 12 minutes on one GPU. Free rollouts remain stable for one year but do not fully capture seasonal cycles. Using idealized data assimilation, we find that chemical observations can constrain the meteorological state and meteorological observations can constrain the chemical state. Inserting only the chemical fields raises the annual mean spatial correlation of 500 hPa temperature from 0.89 to 0.92 and recovers the moisture and circulation pattern of the Indian summer monsoon. Inserting only the meteorological fields raises the 500 hPa OH correlation from 0.89 to 0.93, close to the 0.94 from inserting the chemical fields themselves, and recovers the OH seasonal cycle. Inserting only NO2 columns sampled at TROPOMI pixels gives an OH correlation of 0.93. These relationships likely reflect learned covariances rather than physical coupling, and covariances are what data assimilation uses to let an observation of one variable update the others. AuroraChem therefore provides a new pathway to joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation.
